title: credential containment recovery
question: Why can restoring current files fail while stolen credential artifacts, ticket paths, privileged accounts, or compromised configuration remain active?
scenario: Credential theft before encryption: An attacker obtains a privileged workstation credential, moves laterally, and begins encrypting shared file services.
focalRelation: Peer validation and mutual authentication constrain intermediary paths; credential artifacts enable actions until contained; segmentation limits propagation; backup recovery restores data only when identities, systems, configurations, and integrity are known good.

prediction.prompt: Why can restoring current files fail while stolen credential artifacts, ticket paths, privileged accounts, or compromised configuration remain active?

options.label: Restore files immediately, retain existing privileged sessions, and test only whether users can open documents.
options.feedback: Compromised identities can immediately recontaminate a restored environment.

options.label: Rebuild application servers first, then rotate privileged identities only if later monitoring finds misuse.
options.feedback: Untrusted identities and sessions can recontaminate the restored environment; containment and recovery-plane trust come first.

options.label: Contain credentials and privileged paths, restore into known-good systems, validate integrity, and obtain business and security acceptance.
options.feedback: A current backup restores data; it does not revoke usable credentials, repair peer validation, remove persistence, or prove trustworthy configuration.

prediction.hint: Identify whether the failure compromises credentials, sessions, protocol trust, or service availability.

retry.prompt: A recovery team restores file servers while the same compromised admin accounts still control backup and deployment tooling. What must change?

options.label: Restore the directory backup while leaving stolen privileged sessions and administration routes active.
options.feedback: Recovery also requires protected backup access, known-good systems, prioritization, restoration testing, credential containment, integrity validation, and business and security acceptance.

options.label: Validate restored file hashes but postpone trusted identity and management-path recovery until normal operations resume.
options.feedback: That shortcut ignores the decisive changed fact. Contain and re-establish trusted privileged identity and administration paths before declaring recovery complete; otherwise the attacker can re-encrypt or alter restored systems.

options.label: Re-establish trusted privileged identities and administration paths before recovery acceptance
options.feedback: Correct. Contain and re-establish trusted privileged identity and administration paths before declaring recovery complete; otherwise the attacker can re-encrypt or alter restored systems.

retry.hint: Protect the recovery plane and validate service under trusted administration.

assumptions: Only entities and claims anchored in the canonical unit or explicitly labeled hypothetical scenario are used.
A highlighted path means the learner is inspecting that path; it does not assert the event occurred.
The current source is authoritative for facts; this treatment reorganizes presentation without changing canonical content.
The lesson teaches one bounded decision and does not claim to exhaust every jurisdiction, vendor implementation, architecture, attack, or exception.

treatmentDispositions.rationale: The state model traces a usable stolen credential through privileged lateral access and ransomware impact, then separates credential and path containment from known-good restoration and joint security and business acceptance. The changed case shows why restoring files alone leaves an accepted credential path active.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Clean backups do not make compromised administrator identities trustworthy. Contain and replace credentials and sessions, protect the recovery plane, restore known-good systems, and obtain security and business acceptance.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: The containment-to-restoration chain adds ordering and recontamination risk, but it does not visually cover every intermediary, ticket, credential, and ransomware path promised by the broad title.
